name: Vedic religion
info: The historical Vedic religion, also called Vedism or Brahmanism, was the religion of some Indo-Aryan peoples of the northwest Indian subcontinent and the western Ganges plain in the Vedic period, c. 1500–500 BCE, known from the Vedas and their sacrifices.

facts.origin: the northwest Indian subcontinent (Punjab and the western Ganges plain), in the early Vedic period from c. 1500 BCE, with roots in the Indo-Iranian religion of the Sintashta and Andronovo cultures
facts.founder: none: it grew out of Indo-Iranian religion and the Bactria–Margiana culture, then took shape in the northwest of the subcontinent
facts.scriptures: the Vedas, the four Samhitas with the Brahmanas, Aranyakas and some of the older Upanishads, composed in Vedic Sanskrit and first handed down by oral transmission
facts.followers: none as a religion of its own after the Vedic period, which is held to have ended around 500 BCE; it became Brahmanism and then Hinduism, and some Vedic rituals are still practised today

t: The religion centred on sacrifices and fire rituals recorded in the Vedas, among them the Agnihotra, the Soma rituals and the Ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice, offered to deities such as Indra, Agni and Varuna.
Ancestor worship was an important, perhaps the central, part of the early religion, which mentions an afterlife but not the later doctrines of karma and reincarnation.
In the late Vedic period it developed into Brahmanism, which gave great weight to the priestly Brahmin class and helped to shape contemporary Hinduism, though the two differ significantly.
dyk: The oldest inscriptions in Old Indic, the language of the Rig Veda, were found in northern Syria, where the Mitanni kings took Old Indic throne names and used the term ṛta, meaning cosmic order and truth.

sections.origins:
The historical Vedic religion, also called Vedism or Brahmanism, was the religion of some Indo-Aryan peoples of the northwest Indian subcontinent (Punjab and the western Ganges plain) during the Vedic period, c. 1500–500 BCE. Its roots lie in the Indo-Iranian religion of the Sintashta (c. 2200–1750 BCE) and Andronovo (c. 2000–1150 BCE) cultures of the Eurasian Steppe. According to Anthony, the Old Indic religion probably emerged among Indo-European immigrants in the contact zone between the Zeravshan River and Iran, as a syncretic mixture of old Central Asian and new Indo-European elements. It borrowed distinctive beliefs and practices from the Bactria–Margiana culture, supported by at least 383 non-Indo-European words, among them the god Indra and the ritual drink soma.

The religion then developed in the northwest during the early Vedic period (c. 1500–1100 BCE), influenced by the remnants of the late Indus Valley Civilisation; White (2003) cites three scholars who have emphatically demonstrated that it partly derives from that civilisation. After c. 1100 BCE the Indo-Aryans moved into the Gangetic Plain and became settled farmers, further merging with native cultures, and in the late Vedic period (c. 1100–500 BCE) Brahmanism developed out of it.
sections.beliefs:
The ancient Vedic religion has been described as a complex animistic religion with polytheistic and pantheistic aspects. Ancestor worship was an important, maybe the central, component, with rites such as sraddha, the offering of food to the ancestors. The early layers of the Vedas do not mention karma and rebirth but do mention belief in an afterlife; reincarnation, or saṃsāra, is absent from early texts such as the Rigveda, and its roots lie in the Upanishads of the late Vedic period.

The Rigveda counts 33 devas, eleven each of earth, space and heaven. The pantheon knows two classes, Devas and Asuras; the Devas, among them Mitra, Varuna, Aryaman and Bhaga, are deities of cosmic and social order. Most notable are the heroic Indra, Agni, the sacrificial fire and messenger of the gods, and Soma, the deified sacred drink. A central myth, Rig Veda 1.32, tells how Indra drinks Soma and slays the dragon Vritra, freeing the rivers, the cows and Dawn. Ethics rest on concepts such as ṛta, fixed or settled order and divine law, and satya, which came to mean truthfulness in thought, speech and action.

Rites include fire rituals with oblations (havir), such as the Agnihotra, the Soma rituals, the royal consecration (Rajasuya) and the Ashvamedha. Burial and cremation are both seen from the Rigvedic period.
sections.texts:
The texts of the Vedic period, composed in Vedic Sanskrit, are mainly the four Vedic Samhitas, with the Brahmanas, Aranyakas and some of the older Upanishads also placed in it. Michael Witzel states that the Vedic canon consists of all the texts that originated in and were used by the Vedic schools. The Vedas record the liturgy connected with the rituals and sacrifices. They were at first preserved only by oral transmission, and the earliest recorded manuscript, found in Nepal, dates from the 11th century. They are also part of the scripture of contemporary Hinduism.

The Rigveda is a collection of hymns to various deities, and according to Anthony Indra was the subject of 250 of them, a quarter of the whole. The later layers of the Vedic literature, the Aranyakas and Upanishads, show a different soteriology based on reincarnation and little concern with ancestor rites, and they begin to interpret the earlier rituals philosophically. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (c. 800 BCE) discusses the earliest versions of the karma doctrine. In the Hindu tradition the revered sages of this era include Yajnavalkya, Atri, Bharadvaja, Vasistha, Vishwamitra and Kanva.
sections.spread:
The religion existed in the western Ganges plain in the early Vedic period, and Indo-Aryans entered the Indus valley in multiple waves during the 2nd millennium BCE. Brahmanism took shape in the Ganges basin around c. 1000 BCE. Its emphasis on ritual and the dominant position of Brahmins developed as an ideology in the Kuru-Pancala realm, and it expanded over a wider area after that realm's demise and its incorporation into the Magadha-based empires. It co-existed with local religions such as the Yaksha cults. The eastern Ganges plain was dominated by another Indo-Aryan complex, which rejected the later Brahmanical ideology and gave rise to Jainism, Buddhism and the Maurya Empire.

Brahmanism declined in the post-Vedic period of the Second Urbanisation. The Shramanic movement, the conquests of Magadha, the Nanda and Mauryan empires, and foreign rule in the northwest threatened the income and patronage of rural Brahmins. This was overcome by providing new services and incorporating the non-Vedic Indo-Aryan heritage of the eastern Gangetic plain and local traditions, which gave rise to contemporary Hinduism. This new Brahmanism appealed to rulers and dominated Indian society from the classical age of Hinduism in the early centuries CE.
sections.community:
Brahmanism is loosely so named, in Heesterman's words, because of the religious and legal importance it places on the brāhmaṇa, the priestly class. The Vedic texts were preserved into modern times by the different priestly schools. Post-Vedic texts such as the Dharmasutras and Dharmaśāstras gave prominence to the priestly (Brahmin) caste of society.

In the period 800–200 BCE, which Muesse calls the classical period, traditional religious practices and beliefs were reassessed, and the Brahmins and the rituals they performed no longer enjoyed the same prestige as in the Vedic period. Michaels calls 500–200 BCE a time of ascetic reformism. The non-Vedic śramaṇa traditions existed alongside Brahmanism: they were not direct outgrowths of Vedism but movements with mutual influences with Brahmanical traditions, and Jainism and Buddhism evolved out of them. According to Olivelle, some scholars hold that the renouncer tradition was an organic and logical development of Vedic ideas, while others hold that it emerged from the indigenous non-Aryan population; the debate is longstanding and ongoing.
sections.legacy:
The historical Vedic religion is now generally accepted as a predecessor of modern Hinduism, though the two are not the same: the textual evidence shows differences, such as belief in an afterlife in place of the later reincarnation and saṃsāra. According to Michaels, the Vedic gods declined but did not disappear, local cults were assimilated into the pantheon, and Shiva and Vishnu became more prominent, giving rise to Shaivism and Vaishnavism. The Upanishads gradually evolved into Vedanta, which considers itself the goal of the Vedas, while Mīmāṃsā philosophers argued that the gods have no existence apart from the mantras that name them.

Some practice continues. According to David Knipe, some communities preserve portions of the religion, as in Kerala and Andhra Pradesh, where the Nambudiri Brahmins continue the Śrauta rituals. The Kalash people of northwest Pakistan practise a form of it, though Witzel notes differences, such as fire placed beside the altar instead of in it. In the 19th century western publications held the Vedic religion to be unrelated to Hinduism, while reform movements such as the Brahmo Samaj and Neo-Vedanta urged a return to the Vedas.

summary: The historical Vedic religion was the religion of some Indo-Aryan peoples of the northwest Indian subcontinent and the Ganges plain from c. 1500 to 500 BCE, centred on sacrifices to gods such as Indra and Agni recorded in the Vedas. It developed into Brahmanism and is now generally seen as a predecessor of Hinduism.
references: Arthur Llewellyn Basham, The Origins and Development of Classical Hinduism (Oxford University Press, 1989)
Edwin Bryant, The Quest for the Origins of Vedic Culture: The Indo-Aryan migration debate (Oxford University Press, 2001)
Gavin D. Flood, An Introduction to Hinduism (Cambridge University Press, 1996)
Jan Heesterman, Vedism and Brahmanism (Macmillan Reference, 2005)
notes: Dates: start c. 1500 BCE and end c. 500 BCE follow the article's Vedic period (c. 1500-500 BCE; 'held to have ended around 500 BCE'). The article also says some Vedic rituals are still practised and that the Kalash practise 'a form' of it (Witzel notes differences). I treated the religion as ended with its continuations told in the legacy section; the editor may prefer end null. The faith map therefore stops at 500 BCE and does not draw Kerala, Andhra or the Kalash.

The article's lede says Brahmanism developed 'as an ideology of the Kuru-Panchala realm'; one passage puts Brahmanism's form 'at the Ganges basin around c. 1000 BCE' and another says the late Vedic period is c. 1100-500 BCE. All are in the text.

Left out: the long list of named rituals beyond a few, the Gomedha (cow sacrifice) details and the Purushamedha, which the article lists without comment; the claim that Shinto contains influences (Witzel, 'suggested') is omitted for length; the terminology of 'Brahmanism' as a word coined in the 16th century and Ambedkar's anti-caste use.
'Vedic religion has been described as a complex animistic religion': the article states this without naming a scholar. Anthony's 250 hymns and 383 words are from the article's quotation and sentence.
Event 'c. 800 BCE' is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad's date as the article gives it. Event '11th century' falls after the end year, as the manuscript is a later fact about the texts.
The article's own references and sources lists are empty in the saved text; its one Further reading item is Bronkhorst (2017), an article, so references are left empty.
Faith map: coordinates for the Punjab, the Kuru-Panchala realm (Haryana and the upper Doab), Magadha and the Zeravshan region are my general-geography estimates; the article gives only names.
